description.value: Canada Border Services Agency's compliance-prediction tool. A decision-tree model reads travel-pattern features from a traveller's current and past passages and shows border services officers an indicator when a traveller is highly likely to meet customs obligations. Officers always make the final decision to release or refer.

value.value: Supports border processing at ports of entry — helping officers focus their attention and reducing unnecessary secondary inspections for travellers who are likely compliant.

Accountable agency. The indicator was designed and built in-house by CBSA's data-science team and runs inside the officer platform used at ports of entry; first deployments at ferry and land border crossings from 2026.

Predicts how likely a traveller is to meet customs obligations and may display an indicator to the border services officer. The officer always makes the final decision to release or refer — the indicator is one input among many, and enforcement systems override it.

A decision-tree model chosen for explainability over predictive power. Trained on five years of de-identified passage and enforcement records; accuracy is tracked across sociodemographic groups and monitored in near real time.

Information about the traveller being processed — travel document details, licence plate, travelling party, and referral and enforcement history from CBSA systems. Immigration and enforcement records carry legal and social weight; before scoring, names, dates of birth and document numbers are stripped and travellers are grouped into four-year age bands.
A compliance indicator shown to the officer — or nothing when likelihood is unknown. Kept only for system analysis and never reused to score the same traveller's later passages.
The indicator is not shown to travellers; it appears only on the officer's screen. The tool is not public-facing.
Available to border services officers inside CBSA's internal systems, alongside the other information they already use.

Risk: patterns learned from five years of past referrals and enforcement records could steer officer attention unfairly — echoing historical bias at the border. Mitigation: random referrals are mixed into the training data, model accuracy is tracked across sociodemographic groups on near-real-time dashboards, privacy and GBA Plus assessments were completed, and an officer decides every outcome.
CBSA must post plain-language notice that an automated system is in use across its service channels; this assessment is published on Canada's Open Government portal.

A plain-language description of how the indicator works is published in the Algorithmic Impact Assessment on open.canada.ca. The decision tree was deliberately chosen so its logic can be understood and explained.
The decision to release or refer a traveller is always made by a border services officer, never by the system.

For decisions that deny a service or trigger regulatory action, CBSA must explain in plain language the system's role in the decision and the main factors behind it; the system can produce reasons for its recommendations.
Travellers can request the personal information CBSA holds about them under the Privacy Act, including the passage records the indicator draws on.
